extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of Japanese administrative law and public administration; policymakers and administrative officials
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of Japan's major administrative-procedure-related statutes (PRAMA, AAIHAO, APPI, APA, ACRA) describing their purposes, substantive rules, and procedural obligations for administrative organs on document management, information disclosure, personal data protection, fair dispositions, and administrative appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRAMA: purpose and scope (public records and archives)
rubrics_metrics.description: PRAMA defines its purpose as the proper and efficient management of public administration and the fulfilment of accountability; it regulates public records and archives, including administrative documents, corporate documents, and specific historical archives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter I: purpose and applicable documents. Archives include documents, pictures, and electronic/magnetic records prepared or obtained by employees in the course of duties and held as shared documents; also corporate documents of incorporated administrative agencies and documents transferred to the National Archives as historically important.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRAMA: preparation requirement—verifiability of decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials of administrative organs shall prepare administrative documents to make the process leading to decision-making and the administrative work of the administrative organs verifiable (Article 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparation obligation aims to ensure transparency and allow reconstruction/verification of administrative actions; applies across types of administrative documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRAMA: arrangement/classification and retention-period setting
rubrics_metrics.description: To arrange created documents, officials must classify and name documents, set the retention period and its expiry date, and consolidate closely related documents into one administrative document file (Article 5, para.1.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The head of the administrative organ must decide on transfer or disposal before expiry and may seek guidance from the National Archives' archivist (Article 5, para.5). Classification and retention decisions are part of standardised document management rules established by heads of organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRAMA: preservation and management registers
rubrics_metrics.description: The head must preserve administrative document files until the expiry date of the retention period and must enter classification, name, retention period, expiry date, measures at expiry, and place of retention into administrative document file management registers (Article 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Management registers must be made publicly available under Article 7, supporting transparency and accountability for document holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRAMA: transfer or disposal after retention expiry (PM consent for disposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the retention period has expired, the head must transfer the file to the National Archives or dispose of it; in the case of disposal, the head must obtain prior consent from the prime minister (Article 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfer to National Archives preserves historically important records; disposal is limited and requires central oversight to prevent premature destruction of public records.

rubrics_metrics.name: AAIHAO: right to request disclosure and covered texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may request the disclosure of administrative documents; the AAIHAO defines its purpose as ensuring administrative activities are available to the public and states that texts covered are administrative documents (Articles 1–3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter II defines request procedures and implementation of disclosure decisions; Chapter III defines requests for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: AAIHAO: non-disclosure categories (Article 5 items 1–7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 5 lists non-disclosure information including (generally): (1) information concerning individuals; (2) anonymously processed information of administrative organs; (3) information of juridical persons whose disclosure would likely harm legitimate interests; (4) information likely to harm national security; (5) information that could hinder maintenance of public safety and order; (6) information on deliberations within/among state organs and related bodies; (7) specific information on the affairs/business of state organs, local governments, incorporated administrative agencies, or local incorporated administrative agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories set the limits to disclosure; agencies must assess documents against these items when processing disclosure requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: AAIHAO: decision types and time limit
rubrics_metrics.description: The head decides on disclosure or non-disclosure, including partial disclosure, discretionary disclosure, and refusal to respond to existence. As a rule, the head must make a disclosure decision within 30 days of the request (Article 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial disclosure redacts non-disclosable parts; discretionary disclosure allows disclosure in public interest even if non-disclosure information is recorded; refusal to respond to existence conceals whether a document exists to avoid inadvertent disclosure of protected information.

rubrics_metrics.name: AAIHAO: third-party input and review mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: If a third party’s information is recorded in a requested document, the head may grant that third party an opportunity to submit a written opinion, and third parties must be given opportunity to submit opinions in discretionary disclosure cases (Article 13). Requests for review of disclosure decisions are examined by the Information Disclosure and Personal Information Protection Review Board (MIC) under Article 19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party participation and an independent review board are procedural safeguards to balance interests in disclosure decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: AAIHAO/APA: requirement to state reasons for non-disclosure or redaction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the head makes a non-disclosure decision or when the disclosed document has non-disclosed parts, the head must attach the reasons for the decision (Article 8 of the APA referenced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing reasons enhances accountability and allows requestors to seek review or challenge decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: APPI: scope, integration, and oversight (PPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The integrated APPI applies to public and private sectors (including local governments) after 2021 integration; the Personal Data Protection Commission (PPC) independently monitors compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration unified earlier fragmented legislation (APPIHAO, APPIHIAA) and placed oversight in an independent commission to address cross-border and cross-sector data flow issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: APPI: limitations on collection (minimum necessary and purpose specification)
rubrics_metrics.description: When gathering personal information, the head of an administrative organ is restricted to the minimum necessary to acquire the information (Article 61(2)) and is required to specify the purpose of use and clearly indicate the purpose to those concerned (Articles 61(1), 62).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose specification and minimisation constrain intrusive data collection and require transparency to data subjects about why data are collected.

rubrics_metrics.name: APPI: prohibition on unlawful acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: The head is prohibited from acquiring personal information through unlawful means (Article 64).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bars covert or otherwise illegal methods of obtaining personal data and underpins trust in administrative data handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: APPI: restrictions on use and provision (including cross-border transfers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heads are, in principle, prohibited from inappropriate use (Article 63) and from use or provision for other purposes (Article 69); providing information to a third party located in a foreign country for a purpose other than the original purpose generally requires the consent of the individual (Article 71(1)), except in specified cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions limit secondary uses and international transfers of retained personal information absent consent or statutory exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: APPI: preservation obligations—accuracy, security, breach reporting, staff duties
rubrics_metrics.description: When preserving retained personal information, the head must ensure accuracy (Article 65), take security control measures to prevent leaks (Article 66), and report any leaks to the PPC (Article 68(1)); employees handling personal information are prohibited from notifying others or using such information improperly (Article 67).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational obligations require technical, organisational, and personnel measures to safeguard personal data and provide accountability in case of breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: APPI: data subject rights and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter V provides rights to request disclosure (Article 76(1)), corrections (Article 90(1)), and suspensions (Article 98(1)); any person may request disclosure or correction of their personal information and may seek review under the ACRA or administrative litigation under the Administrative Case Litigation Act if unsatisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory rights set administrative remedies and pathways to challenge mishandling of personal information.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA: overall purpose and covered procedural areas
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the APA is to promote protection of public rights and interests by improving fairness and transparency of administrative decision-making; it sets procedures for dispositions upon application (Ch. II), adverse dispositions (Ch. III), administrative guidance (Ch. IV), notifications (Ch. V), and public comment procedures (Ch. VI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA establishes both pre-procedural and procedural protections across common administrative actions; public comment procedures were added in the 2005 amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA Chapter II: application-processing obligations (review standards, processing time, commencement, reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative agencies with authority to process applications must set review standards as concretely as possible and make them public (Article 5); endeavour to establish and publish a standard period of processing applications (Article 6); begin to process an application without delay when received (Article 7); and if rejecting an application, provide its reason in principle (Article 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These requirements address problems of opaque review standards, arbitrary refusal/neglect, and lack of reasons for rejections, promoting predictability and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA Chapter III: pre-procedure for adverse dispositions (standards, hearings, explanations, reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: For dispositions limiting rights or imposing duties, administrative agencies must endeavour to set standards and make them public (Article 12); before making an adverse disposition citizens should be given hearings or written explanations (Article 13); hearings allow face-to-face statements, documentary evidence, and questioning; explanations permit written submissions; and when making a disposition, agencies must provide reasons in principle (Article 14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-procedural rights (hearings/explanations) improve predictability, permit citizen input, and ensure decisions are reasoned and contestable.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA Chapter IV: administrative guidance protections (non-coercion and information duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative guidance is simple guidance without coercive power (Article 32(1)); administrative organs must not treat citizens unfavourably for refusing it (Article 32(2)); the agent imposing guidance must provide key information to the subject citizen; citizens may request suspension of guidance they believe does not conform to laws (Article 36-2); and citizens may require administrative guidance to correct illegal states (Chapter IV-2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules limit informal pressure masquerading as guidance and provide remedies where guidance is abused.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACRA: purpose, methods, and scope of administrative appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: ACRA's purpose is to protect citizens’ rights and ensure proper administration by providing a simple, prompt, and fair system of administrative appeal; three methods exist—request for review, request for re-investigation, and request for re-examination. Subjects of review include dispositions and omissions by administrative agencies (Articles 2–3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACRA functions as the post-procedure complement to APA pre-procedures; omission (failure to act) is treated as reviewable.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACRA: review agency designation and exceptional cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A review agency is generally a higher administrative agency than the administrative agency reaching the disposition, although there are exceptional cases where the agency that reached the disposition may serve as the review agency (Article 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designating a higher agency as reviewer aims to ensure impartial review, but statutory exceptions exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACRA: procedural stages and fairness safeguards (review officer, exclusion grounds, council consultation)
rubrics_metrics.description: General review procedure: (1) appointment of a review officer from among staff to preside (Article 9), with statutory grounds for exclusion of staff involved in the disposition or having interest (Article 9(2)); the review officer marshals arguments and collects evidence from the agency, requestor, and participants, then drafts a determination; (2) the review agency consults councils to ensure fairness (Article 43)—central government agencies consult the Administrative Complaint Review Board (MIC); (3) the review agency makes determinations referring to the draft and council report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural safeguards include exclusion rules to avoid conflicts of interest, evidentiary collection by a designated officer, and independent council review to enhance fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACRA: types of determinations and legal effects (dismissal with/without prejudice, upholding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations are classified into dismissal without prejudice (formal defects), dismissal with prejudice (no grounds after substantive discussion), and upholding (disposition judged illegal or unjust). If dismissed, the state of disposition continues; if upheld, the disposition is corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The taxonomy clarifies procedural vs. substantive grounds and consequences for administrative acts; 'upholding' triggers corrective action by the administrative agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrelated operation of laws and delegation to administrative organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Each law entrusts operational details to respective administrative organs; laws prescribe general rules while individual organs process cases, relying on staff discretion and internal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This delegation is rational for differing agency activities but creates risks tied to staff skills, ethics, and internal operations—highlighting the need for effective management systems, clear division of work, organisational culture reforms, and staff training.
